title: Medical wards: protected night repositioning rounds for pressure injuries, landmark lead unverified, renamed record quarantined
notes: Adversarial path on a clear QI question (routing explicit qi-pdsa from 'quality improvement project using PDSA cycles' and 'run charts'). A fixture search returns seven records with abstracts. The first scan reply (shape discovery) carries three leads: a model-labelled 'landmark' ratio study with the invented DOI 10.5555/nsj.2018.0777, which is appended and must stay unverified with no checks (G3); a lead that reuses the id of retrieved record 2 (ev-1ihlm0s) but renames the uncontrolled before-after report as a multicentre controlled trial that 'eliminated' injuries, which must be quarantined with issue id-collision while record 2 keeps its title, provenance, missing DOI and label (A2 item 6; D1, S1); and a sensor report appended as a lead with methodQuality null. The reply's certainty is an explicit null, so certainty stays unassessed until the appraisal. The second scan reply (shape appraisal) annotates the seven records, again tries to retitle record 2 (the title key is dropped with an issue, the stored title unchanged) and records claims c1 to c4; certainty 'low'. The design decision rests on c1 to c3 only; the float nurse gate is unknown, so acceptance gives selection accepted and action blocked. Reload and reopen follow the last stage. Unlike a lead that echoes a retrieved record with an invented DOI, here the colliding lead changes the record's title and design, and the landmark lead is a separate, non-colliding invention. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts, computed by the generator script: DOI hash for records 1, 3, 5, 6 (ev-0bok56v, ev-0uhk5zi, ev-0aphgus, ev-0ekr4am); titleYearKey hash for records 2, 4, 7 (ev-1ihlm0s, ev-0clsgbr, ev-1tyuu4i). Requires D1 and S1 (append and quarantine), S13 (appraisal), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text). Catches: a lead that renames or overwrites a retrieved record, a model label or DOI treated as verification, identity edits through the appraisal, and a decision resting on unretrieved leads.

inputs.need:
I am the clinical nurse specialist for tissue viability at a 420-bed general hospital. Two medical wards, 7A and 7B, have the highest rates of hospital-acquired pressure injuries in the hospital, and most injuries are first found on the morning after a night shift. The staffing roster shows that on nearly half of nights these wards run with one registered nurse for more than seven patients, and the night nurses tell us that two-hourly repositioning is the first thing to slip when the ward is busy. We cannot fund more nurses, but the night bank can sometimes release a float nurse.

We want to run a quality improvement project using PDSA cycles to test a protected night repositioning round: at 23:00, 02:00 and 05:00 a named nurse, or the float nurse when the ratio is worse than one to seven, repositions and checks the skin of every patient at high risk, and the risk score is reassessed at the evening handover. We would track pressure injuries on run charts and look separately at nights with poor staffing.

The board has asked me what the evidence says about staffing levels and pressure injuries, because a colleague keeps quoting a large multicentre study that supposedly proved a fixed ratio prevents most injuries, and I cannot find it. I need help with an aim statement, a measure that is not distorted by how injuries are reported, balancing measures for the night shift, and how to present rare events without overclaiming.
inputs.constraints: No additional nursing posts; any float nurse comes from the existing night bank. Changes must fit the electronic care plan without new build. Results are reported at ward level only, never by individual nurse.
localFacts: Wards 7A and 7B (28 beds each) recorded 41 hospital-acquired pressure injuries of category 2 or worse in the last 12 months.
On 46 percent of nights last year, wards 7A and 7B ran with one registered nurse for more than seven patients, according to the staffing roster.
The hospital quality committee registered the project as quality improvement on 2026-09-02 (registration QI-2026-054); no REB review is required.
The tissue viability team inspects the skin of every patient on both wards once a week, and all pressure injuries are entered in the incident system within 24 hours.

records.title: Night-shift nurse staffing and hospital-acquired pressure injuries: an observational study across 24 medical wards
records.authors: Achterberg-Kimani L, Solberg-Nwosu P, Fairley-Ortega D
records.abstract: We linked shift-level staffing records to hospital-acquired pressure injuries on 24 medical wards over two years. Each additional patient per registered nurse on night shifts was associated with an 11 percent higher incidence of category 2 or worse pressure injuries after adjustment for patient acuity and ward. Day-shift staffing showed a weaker association. The association was strongest on wards where most patients were at high risk. Because staffing and acuity move together, residual confounding is likely, and the study cannot show that a fixed ratio would prevent injuries. Wards with a float nurse available at night had fewer missed repositioning episodes recorded in care plans.

records.title: Protected night repositioning rounds on two medical wards: a before-after improvement report
records.abstract: Two medical wards introduced protected night repositioning rounds at fixed times, led by a named nurse, with a float nurse joining when staffing fell below a set level. We compared pressure injuries in the nine months before and the nine months after the change. Category 2 or worse injuries fell from 3.1 to 1.9 per 1,000 patient-days. Completion of the night rounds was recorded on 84 percent of nights. Nurses reported that fixed times made repositioning harder to postpone. The comparison is uncontrolled, a new mattress contract started during the second period, and injuries were counted from incident reports.

records.title: Pressure injury prevention bundles in acute hospital care: a systematic review
records.authors: Kaur-Brennan S, Delacroix-Ansah M, Petrov-Holt J, Nakashima-Obi F
records.abstract: We searched four databases for controlled and uncontrolled studies of prevention bundles in adult acute care. Thirty-one studies met the criteria; 26 reported fewer pressure injuries after a bundle was introduced, but only five had a concurrent control. Repositioning schedules, risk reassessment and skin inspection were the most common components. Effects were larger in studies that measured injuries by incident reports than in studies that used direct skin inspection. Most studies were at high risk of bias, and none separated the effect of staffing from the effect of the bundle. The review supports bundles as change ideas rather than as proven interventions.

records.title: Weekly skin inspection compared with incident reporting for measuring pressure injury incidence
records.abstract: On six wards we compared pressure injuries found at weekly skin inspection by a tissue viability nurse with injuries recorded in the incident reporting system. Incident reports captured 64 percent of the category 2 or worse injuries found at inspection. Capture was lower for injuries on the heels and for patients discharged within a week. Reporting rose during periods of improvement activity, which would make an improvement project look worse at first when measured by incident reports. The authors recommend weekly inspection as the outcome measure for improvement work and incident reports as a secondary source.

records.title: Float nurse deployment when night ratios exceed a threshold: effects on missed care in medical wards
records.abstract: Four medical wards deployed a float nurse on nights when the ratio exceeded one nurse to seven patients. Using care-plan records, we compared missed care on nights with and without a float nurse over one year. Missed repositioning was recorded on 18 percent of high-risk patient-nights without a float nurse and 9 percent with one. Missed medication doses showed a similar but smaller difference. Float nurses were available on 61 percent of the nights that met the threshold. Nights were not allocated at random, and ward managers requested float nurses more often for the busiest nights.

records.title: Skin tone and the detection of early pressure injury: an observational study of nurse assessment
records.abstract: We compared ward nurses' skin assessments with assessments by tissue viability specialists in 540 adult inpatients. Category 1 pressure injuries were missed by ward nurses in 38 percent of patients with darker skin tones and 14 percent of patients with lighter skin tones. Missed early injuries more often progressed to category 2 or worse within a week. Assessment that included touch for warmth and firmness, not only colour, reduced the difference. The study used a small number of specialist assessors in one hospital, and skin tone was recorded by the assessors.

records.title: Run chart rules for rare adverse events in ward improvement projects
records.abstract: Improvement teams often plot rare adverse events such as pressure injuries or falls with injury as weekly counts, which produces charts dominated by zeros. We simulated ward-level data and compared run charts of weekly rates with charts of the number of patient-days between events. With fewer than two events per ward per week, charts of patient-days between events detected a halving of the event rate about six weeks earlier than weekly run charts and gave fewer false signals. We recommend charts of time or patient-days between events for rare events, with the counting rule fixed before baseline.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Worse night staffing is associated with more pressure injuries, and a float nurse is associated with less missed repositioning, but neither study shows that a fixed ratio prevents injuries. Protected night rounds were followed by fewer injuries in one uncontrolled report. Incident reports undercount injuries found at weekly inspection, and early injuries are missed more often in darker skin. Rare events are better charted as patient-days between events. The multicentre ratio study quoted to the board was offered only as an unverified model lead and was not retrieved.
response.gradeRationale: Observational and uncontrolled before-after evidence, one review of studies at high risk of bias; consistent in direction, with serious confounding by acuity.

response.reading: Night staffing, repositioning and early detection form one causal chain: when a ward is short, repositioning slips (c1), and injuries that start as category 1 are missed, more often in darker skin (c4), until they are found at category 2. A protected round targets the middle of the chain (c2); the float nurse targets its start. Measurement sits outside the chain but can distort it, because incident reports undercount and rise with attention (c3). The multicentre ratio study quoted to the board remains an unverified lead.

response.overview: Ward QI project on 7A and 7B using the Model for Improvement: a baseline year from existing weekly inspection data, then three PDSA cycles from November 2026 to April 2027 testing a protected night repositioning round, first without and then with a float nurse on poorly staffed nights, and finally with touch-based skin assessment.

response.procedures: Cycle 1 (November and December): round on 7A only, no float nurse. Cycle 2 (January and February): both wards, float nurse requested on qualifying nights. Cycle 3 (March and April): touch-based assessment added. Weekly skin inspection by tissue viability continues unchanged as the measurement source; the night nurse in charge records round completion and float availability on a ward sheet each night. Fortnightly huddle reviews the charts.

response.designSummary: Time-ordered measurement of a rare event with a chart of patient-days between injuries (g-chart) as the primary display and monthly rate charts as secondary.
response.sampleSize: The two wards have about 18,800 patient-days a year, so 41 injuries give a baseline of about 2.2 per 1,000 patient-days and a median of about 460 patient-days between injuries. Weekly counts would average fewer than one injury, so a weekly run chart would be mostly zeros. Over six months of cycles about 9,400 patient-days are expected; if the rate halves, about 10 injuries would occur instead of 20, and a g-chart would show a signal when two or more consecutive intervals exceed the upper limit or eight intervals lie above the baseline median. Six months is therefore the minimum period for a credible signal.
response.primaryAnalysis: g-chart of patient-days between successive category 2 or worse injuries, centre line and limits from the baseline year, with pre-specified rules: a single interval above the upper limit, or eight consecutive intervals above the baseline median. Limits are recalculated only after a sustained shift.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Monthly u-charts of injury rates split by nights worse or better than one nurse to seven; run charts of round completion, float availability, late night doses and patients woken.
response.missingData: Weeks without inspection are annotated and the patient-days are counted without assumed injuries; nights without a completion sheet are counted as not recorded, not as completed.
response.multiplicity: One primary chart carries the aim; other charts are descriptive and not tested.

response.summary: Rare events charted as patient-days between injuries; about six months of cycles needed for a credible signal.

response.risks: Minimal: repositioning is standard care. Risks are sleep disturbance, time taken from other night care, and blame of individual nurses for injuries.
response.consent: The round is care, not research; patients are told about it and may ask not to be woken for a round, which is recorded and respected. Staff take part as normal work.
response.data: Inspection and completion data are held by tissue viability with bed numbers and dates only; reports are at ward level; no nurse is identified.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with darker skin tones, patients with cognitive impairment or delirium who cannot report pain, and patients with limited English are at risk of later detection. Touch-based assessment is part of cycle 3, injuries are reported by skin tone category, and interpreters are used when patients are asked about being woken.
response.effectiveness: Success is a sustained lengthening of the interval between injuries with stable late-dose and waking measures.
response.efficiency: Uses existing staff and inspection; the float nurse comes from the night bank when available.
response.costs: Recording sheets and staff time; no new budget.
response.partnerships: Night nurses from both wards, the night bank manager, tissue viability, and two patient partners from the hospital's patient panel.
response.rebPath: Registered by the hospital quality committee as quality improvement (QI-2026-054, 2026-09-02); no REB review required. Publication would follow SQUIRE 2.0 and the journal's policy for QI reports.
response.limitations: Two wards; uncontrolled; float availability outside the team's control.
response.summary: Minimal-risk QI with ward-level reporting, a right to decline night waking, and equity reporting by skin tone.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners and two night nurses review the round's wording to patients and the waking question; the night bank manager joins the fortnightly huddle once a month.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the wards' patient comment cards are read for mentions of night-time care.

response.title: A protected night repositioning round to reduce hospital-acquired pressure injuries on two medical wards: a quality improvement project
response.abstract: Problem: 41 category 2 or worse pressure injuries in a year on two medical wards, most found after night shifts, with poor night staffing on almost half of nights. Intervention: a protected night repositioning round with handover risk reassessment, a float nurse when available and touch-based skin assessment, tested in three PDSA cycles. Measures: patient-days between injuries found at weekly inspection, rates by night staffing, round completion and balancing measures. Results will follow the cycles.
response.introduction: Night staffing is associated with pressure injuries, and protected repositioning has been followed by fewer injuries in an uncontrolled report. The multicentre ratio study quoted locally could not be traced by the recorded search.
response.methods: Model for Improvement; three PDSA cycles from November 2026 to April 2027; outcome from weekly skin inspection with a fixed counting rule; g-chart with pre-specified rules; registration QI-2026-054.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the g-chart, staffing-stratified rates, round completion and balancing measures, with injuries by skin tone category.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret any signal against co-interventions, state what the project shows about poorly staffed nights, and avoid causal claims about staffing ratios.
response.limitations: Two wards; uncontrolled; rare events; float nurse availability outside the team's control.
response.conclusion: To be written after the cycles; limited to these wards' injuries and the round's delivery.
response.summary: SQUIRE-structured draft with results left empty.
